root.note: šabbāṯ. Some trace it further to Akkadian šapattum, but Wiktionary marks that link as uncertain.

history: Sábado isn't named after a god. It comes from Hebrew shabbat, ‘rest’, the seventh day of the Jewish week, from Friday night to Saturday night. Greek made it sábbaton, Late Latin sabbătum, and Christian Spanish kept it. So every sábado you are using a word from the Bible's day of rest. English Saturday went the other way and kept the Roman god Saturn. Italian sabato and Portuguese sábado share its origin, and French samedi is believed to come from a related Latin form. Note the written accent: sábado, stress on the first syllable, with no capital letter.
historyEinfach: Sábado means ‘Saturday’. The word comes from Hebrew shabbat, ‘rest’. It is the Jewish day of rest. Greek and Latin took the word, and it came to Spanish. English Saturday is different: it is the day of the Roman god Saturn. Spanish writes days of the week with a small letter: el sábado.

elsewhere.text: The Hebrew word for the day of rest reached Spanish through Greek and Latin, and became the name of a weekday.
English took its Saturday from the Roman god, not from the day of rest.
Samedi is believed to come from an unrecorded Latin form, a relative of sábado.
